There’s more than one way to expand your reach in the aftermarket.

- Business Growth: A Constant Risk vs. Opportunity Calculation

- New Technology Reshapes Aftermarket Parts and Service Demand

- ADAS Complexity Reshapes Aftermarket Product Strategy

A company can add locations, enter new markets and build its distribution network over time. It can also acquire an established business or partner with a network that already has the relationships and infrastructure in place.

Recent aftermarket moves show both approaches in action. Parts Authority acquired NPW Companies, while Dana expanded its relationship with VIPAR Heavy Duty. STILLEN also joined The AAM Group as a supporting supplier partner.

The deals vary in size and structure, but they have something in common: Each gives the companies involved an opportunity to reach more of the aftermarket through an established network.

Expanding Through Acquisition

NPW brought 46 locations to Parts Authority, increasing the combined network to nearly 325 locations. The acquisition also expanded Parts Authority’s reach into five new states.

That kind of growth would take considerable time to build location by location. Through the acquisition, Parts Authority gains an existing footprint, along with the infrastructure and customer relationships NPW has developed.

NPW also brings a broad portfolio of traditional, engine and performance parts. Its catalog includes more than 1 million part numbers from more than 700 brands. The acquisition adds product depth along with geographic reach.

For customers, a larger network can also put more inventory closer to the businesses that need it.

Reaching Customers Through Partnerships

Acquisition isn’t the only way to gain access to an established network.

Dana’s distribution agreement with VIPAR Heavy Duty will expand access to Dana’s commercial vehicle products across the VIPAR Heavy Duty Family of Companies network. The agreement will increase product availability for distributors, fleets and repair facilities across North America.

The agreement primarily focuses on Spicer drivetrain products and the Victor Reinz commercial vehicle sealing portfolio.

Instead of building that additional distribution footprint itself, Dana can use an established network to put its products within reach of more customers.

The approach differs from an acquisition, but the goal is similar: using an existing distribution footprint to expand market reach.

The STILLEN partnership with The AAM Group provides another variation.

STILLEN joined AAM as a supporting supplier partner for its Total Truck Centers and Parts Pro programs. The relationship connects STILLEN with a nationwide network of independent aftermarket businesses.

The partnership also goes beyond product availability. AAM will support STILLEN through email campaigns, customer promotions, digital marketing materials and training opportunities.

That highlights another role these networks can play. Suppliers need distribution, but they also need ways to provide product information and support to the businesses selling their products.

As the aftermarket continues to evolve, acquisitions and partnerships will remain two ways companies can strengthen their networks and reach new customers. The strategies may differ from one company to another, but distribution remains at the center. Ultimately, success still depends on connecting products, information and customers efficiently.

When customers request aggressive brake pads, the term can have several meanings. Some want sharper freeway stops. Others want more confidence on winding roads or greater control while towing. Some simply prefer a firmer and more responsive pedal.

- Continental Tire’s Brian Beierwaltes on Driving Brand Promise

- EV Safety: What You Need to Know

- Why Damaged O2 Sensors Cause More Problems Than You Think

Terms such as “aggressive,” “high performance,” and “racing” often appear in marketing. However, they do not always describe what the customer needs.

Technicians should begin by asking questions rather than recommending a product.

Ask About Current Brake Performance

The first question is: “What do you like or dislike about your current brakes?”

Long stopping distances, a soft pedal or inconsistent braking may not indicate a pad problem. Hydraulic faults, caliper issues or master cylinder problems can create similar symptoms.

Customers may incorrectly attribute those symptoms to the brake pads.

Technicians should also ask when the brakes were last serviced. A customer who cannot remember may not need a high-performance pad immediately.

In many cases, a premium replacement pad can restore like-new braking feel. This option may meet the customer’s needs without moving to a more aggressive product.

Define Expectations for Aggressive Brake Pads

The next question is: “What do you expect an aggressive brake pad to do?”

Advertising, online forums and articles may shape customer expectations before the visit. The technician’s role is to guide those expectations toward the correct application.

After identifying the customer’s preferences, ask how the vehicle operates each day. Determine whether it sees mostly highway driving, winding roads or stop-and-go traffic.

Also ask whether the customer regularly tows or hauls. These answers show how often the brakes experience heavy use.

They also indicate whether the brakes usually operate cold or at higher temperatures.

Discuss Noise, Dust and Pad Life

Technicians should explain potential differences in brake noise, dust, pedal feel and pad life. This discussion can prevent misunderstandings and avoidable comebacks.

A brake pad recommendation should follow the complete conversation. Some customers may already prefer a specific brand.

Others may rely on the technician’s recommendation. In either case, product research helps separate verified performance characteristics from marketing claims.

CVSA releases 2026 Roadcheck results highlighting vehicle and driver violations

Roadcheck inspectors found 19% of commercial motor vehicles had out-of-service violations.

Cargo securement ranked fourth among North America’s top vehicle out-of-service violations.

Inspectors affixed 17,680 CVSA decals to vehicles that passed eligible safety inspections.

The Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance (CVSA) recently released the results of its 2026 International Roadcheck , with inspectors conducting 54,575 commercial motor vehicle and driver inspections across North America during the three-day event. The results show that 81% of vehicles and 94.2% of drivers inspected had no out-of-service (OOS) violations.

The alliance reported that inspectors placed 10,350 vehicles and 3,184 drivers OOS. Inspectors also affixed 17,680 CVSA decals to eligible vehicles that passed comprehensive safety inspections without critical mechanical or OOS violations.

Vehicle inspection results

Inspectors conducted 44,047 Level I, II, and V vehicle inspections and identified 13,924 OOS vehicle violations. Brake systems were the most frequently cited violation, with 3,379 violations accounting for 24.3% of all vehicle out-of-service violations.

Tires ranked second with 2,914 violations, followed by 20% defective brakes with 2,072. Cargo securement ranked fourth with 1,724 violations, while lights accounted for 1,659.

Combining brake systems and defective brakes, there were 5,451 total brake-related violations.

Cargo securement was the vehicle violation focus for this year’s Roadcheck. Inspectors identified violations involving freight that was inadequately restrained, immobilized, locked, secured, tied down, packed, or monitored.

Driver inspection results

Inspectors conducted 53,271 Level I, II, and III inspections involving commercial motor vehicle drivers. A total of 3,184 drivers were placed OOS.

The most common driver out-of-service violation was not having a medical card, accounting for 1,072 violations, or 27% of all driver out-of-service violations. Hours-of-service (HOS) violations ranked second with 929, followed by no commercial driver’s license with 620.

English language proficiency (ELP) violations accounted for 361 driver out-of-service violations, while false records of duty status accounted for 266.

ELD tampering, falsification, or manipulation was the driver violation focus for 2026. Inspectors issued 146 out-of-service orders for ELD tampering, making it the seventh most-cited driver OOS violation in North America.

CVSA releases 2026 human trafficking awareness results to strengthen prevention efforts

CVSA schedules Brake Safety Week for August 23–29 to improve brake compliance

Hazardous materials inspections

Inspectors conducted 2,590 inspections of vehicles transporting hazardous materials or dangerous goods (HM/DG). Those inspections resulted in 368 vehicle and 63 driver OOS violations.

Placarding was the top HM/DG out-of-service violation, with 40 violations accounting for 28.4% of all HM/DG OOS violations. Loading violations ranked second with 38, followed by shipping papers with 25.

What this means for the trucking industry

The 2026 Roadcheck results point fleets toward several areas that warrant continued attention, particularly brakes, tires, cargo securement, driver credentials, HOS, and ELD records.

The concentration of brake-related violations also reinforces the value of thorough preventive maintenance and pre-trip inspections. For fleet managers, the ELD findings show that compliance extends beyond having the required technology in the cab—accurate records and proper use remain critical.

The results also give fleets a practical checklist for preparing vehicles and drivers for roadside inspections, with mechanical condition, documentation, cargo securement, and electronic logging practices all affecting compliance.

The AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety’s newly released 2025 American Driving Survey shows gas and diesel vehicles continued to account for most driving in 2025 at 89.5% of all trips, down from 91% in 2024.

However, a research brief states that hybrid and electric vehicle use did increase last year, representing 7.4% (up 1% from 2024) and 3.1% of trips (up 0.6% from 2024), respectively.

AAA Foundation says the survey is meant to quantify the U.S. population’s daily driving and compare the results with previous years. A research brief explores trends in driving behavior by vehicle age and vehicle type, including differences across population groups. The survey was conducted between Jan. 1, 2023, and Dec. 31, 2025.

U.S. drivers collectively made 232 billion trips, spent 95 billion hours driving, and traveled 2.76 trillion miles last year.

Those results were projected to the national population based on a survey of 5,100 participants whose answers showed they made an average of 2.40 driving trips per day, spent 59.3 minutes driving, and traveled 28.6 miles daily.

“Driving patterns in 2025 remained similar to those observed in previous years, with only observed changes in travel exposure and vehicle characteristics,” the brief states. “Drivers traveled slightly fewer miles and spent slightly less time driving compared with 2024, while newer vehicles and vehicles with hybrid or electric powertrains continued to represent a growing share of trips. EV use remained limited but was associated with longer trips compared with conventional vehicles. Continued monitoring of travel behavior, vehicle characteristics, and demographic differences remains important for understanding changes in mobility patterns and their implications for traffic safety in the United States.”

Researchers found that 95% of U.S. residents ages 16 and older reported driving at least occasionally in 2025, a slight increase from 2024.

As in previous years, drivers ages 35–49 reported the most daily trips, driving time, and mileage, while drivers ages 16–19 reported the least, according to the brief.

“Driving prevalence increased across most age groups between 2024 and 2025,” the brief states. “The largest significant increase was observed among 16- to 19-year-olds, rising from 83.1% to 91.4%, and for 25- to 34-year-olds (95.5%). Smaller increases were observed across the remaining age groups, with driving rates exceeding 90% for all age categories.”

“Male drivers reported more trips, driving time, and miles than female drivers. “Drivers in the South reported the highest daily driving time and mileage, while drivers in the West reported the lowest. “Drivers with a bachelor’s degree or higher reported more trips and greater driving time and mileage than other education groups. “The distribution of driving trips by vehicle age continued to shift toward newer vehicles, with vehicles aged 0–4 years accounting for the largest share of trips (39.3%), up from 34% in 2024 and 27% in 2023.”

“Male drivers reported more trips, driving time, and miles than female drivers.

“Drivers in the South reported the highest daily driving time and mileage, while drivers in the West reported the lowest.

“Drivers with a bachelor’s degree or higher reported more trips and greater driving time and mileage than other education groups.

“The distribution of driving trips by vehicle age continued to shift toward newer vehicles, with vehicles aged 0–4 years accounting for the largest share of trips (39.3%), up from 34% in 2024 and 27% in 2023.”

AAA Foundation says that EV trips had the longest average duration and distance compared with gas/diesel and hybrid vehicles. Gas/diesel vehicles averaged 24.3 minutes and 11.8 miles per trip, while hybrids averaged 25 minutes and 12.4 miles.

EV trips had the longest average duration and distance, averaging 30.1 minutes and 13.8 miles per trip.

Hybrid and EV use was highest among drivers with a bachelor’s degree or higher and among drivers located in the West.

As for road trips, 30.1% of survey respondents reported taking at least one road trip in the previous four weeks, with an average one-way trip length of 234.8 miles. Gas/diesel vehicles remained the predominant vehicle type across all groups, accounting for more than 90% of trips in most categories.

NASHVILLE, Tenn. – TMD Friction has announced the launch of a new friction material for heavy-duty applications using air disc brakes. The new material is designated Textar T3080 and is engineered for applications where high torque levels are required to meet the FMVSS121 Stopping Distance Regulations. In addition, TMD says Textar T3080 already meets the 2014 and 2021 “Better Brakes Rules” environmental regulations for heavy metals and copper content, an upcoming challenge facing the brake friction industry. Multiple friction levels are required to best optimize pad and rotor life for different truck, tractor and trailer applications and T3080 rounds out Textar’s North American Air Disc Brake Friction product portfolio by adding a material for the most extreme torque applications on the road, TMD says. As the North American heavy truck market shifts more to air disc brakes, a key issue is the cost justification of this new brake product. Tom Green, managing director of TMD Friction North America noted, “If disc brakes are to replace drum brakes in large numbers, their acceptance will be based on initial and life cycle costs when compared to drum brakes. Disc brakes cost more upfront, so it is critical to maximize life and minimize operational costs. Textar now has four different friction materials for the North American air disc brake market. Each is designed to optimize the life cycle costs for a particular duty cycle.” Jim Clark, TMD’s director of engineering for NAFTA, added, “You don’t have to look far to find examples of multiple levels of brake lining friction to optimize brake life. Current drum brake linings on North American commercial vehicles have three distinct friction levels that rate at 20,000 lbs., 23,000 lbs., and the higher GAWRs. While the formulation, quality and consistency of any friction material product has a lot to do with its wear properties, a basic rule of friction science simply states, ‘the lower the friction, the longer the life of the friction material’. This also applies to the rotor. The lower the friction of the disc pad material, the longer the rotor will last. Besides improved life, having multiple friction levels is the best way to address brake balance problems the disc brake faces when mated to drum brakes. We have already seen disc/drum brake compatibility as an issue in working with several large fleets.” In dynamometer wear tests, two air disc friction materials with different effective coefficients of friction were tested by TMD. Results showed that with a higher effective coefficient of friction (0.38) the pad wears anywhere from 40 percent to 80 percent more than the lower friction pad (0.28). “Given the large difference in wear rates between the high and low ends of the typical friction range, it is important to select the appropriate friction level in order to maximize pad life, rotor life and maintain safety,” said Clark. “This is why TMD has developed multiple friction materials for North America, Textar – T3050, T3070 and T3080. They cover all the GAWR ratings. We also offer a special material, one of the European market leaders Textar T7400, for the transit bus and refuse truck market.”

CVSA schedules Brake Safety Week for August 23–29 to improve brake compliance

CVSA Brake Safety Week runs August 23–29 with roadside inspections across the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.

Inspectors will focus on brake drums and rotors, key components impacting stopping power and road safety.

Fleets should prioritize pre-trip brake checks to avoid out-of-service violations during enforcement week.

The Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance (CVSA) revealed Brake Safety Week will take place August 23–29 to focus on commercial motor vehicle brake safety across North America. The alliance, which oversees coordinated roadside safety programs in Canada, Mexico, and the U.S., said trained inspectors will conduct routine inspections focused on brake systems and components.

Inspectors will pay particular attention to drums and rotors during this year’s brake-safety focus. Brake drum and rotor issues can affect braking efficiency and may result in debris dislodging from vehicles, potentially causing damage or injuries.

Vehicles found with brake-related out-of-service violations, or any other out-of-service violations, will be removed from service until corrected.

In addition to inspections, Brake Safety Week also emphasizes education and awareness. Inspectors and officials will engage with drivers, motor carriers, and mechanics to highlight the importance of proactive vehicle maintenance in reducing crashes and improving safety outcomes.

Motor carriers and drivers are encouraged to complete pre- and post-trip inspections to ensure all brake components are operating properly before vehicles are in service.

Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen celebrated the opening of a new automotive career training center at Central Community College’s Hastings Campus earlier this week.

“This is a significant investment in Nebraska’s future, giving more students the opportunity to gain hands-on training, develop valuable skills, and build rewarding careers right here in our state,” Pillen said in a social media post .

The new Gosper Building will house automotive technology and autobody programs, according to a post made by Central Community College .

The $20 million, 42,000 square-foot building will replace the college’s old facility, which had limitations to industry training methods, local news station NTV says .

“The program over the last couple of years has been growing. Every single year we’ve had, we’ve seen more enrollment, higher enrollment. So we needed to expand our capacity for tools, equipment and instruction.” First Year Automotive Instructor Nick Kelley told NTV.  “There’s an increased interest in automotive technology, cars are getting more technologically advanced so we need better training and more training. There’s still people that really like, really enjoy working on cars.”

The new building can hold 70 automotive students and 20 autobody students, the news station reports. The college offers certifications, diplomas and associate degrees in automotive technology, Auto body technology and other fields.

“I could not be more proud of what our community colleges do for workforce development and creating extraordinary careers – extraordinary careers that you can get developed, in some instances, certification in eight weeks,” NTV reports the Governor during the groundbreaking ceremony.

NTV previously reported that the facility will feature five new classrooms, a welding lab and capacity to work on electric vehicles and modern technology.

The U.S. economy is short roughly 140,000 skilled technicians a year , and the gap is widening, with 73,354 new collision repair entrant technicians needed by 2029, according to the TechForce Foundation’s new “Technician Supply, Demand & Opportunity Report.”

Across those 10 sectors, employers will need 241,842 new technicians per year through 2029, the report finds, compared with 101,743 students who graduated from technical schools and community colleges last year. TechForce found that the collision repair sector sees the highest turnover of the 10 analyzed at 60.7%.

Howat said the company’s engineering-driven approach is what differentiates its belt drive tensioners. With a history of innovation dating back to its founder’s invention of the first belt tensioner in 1979, Litens has developed an extensive portfolio of patented technologies. Unlike manufacturers focused primarily on individual components, Litens engineers complete belt drive systems, with the tensioner and pulley system playing a central role in their operation. Howat emphasized that this engineering expertise and problem-solving approach allow Litens to deliver innovative tensioning solutions to the aftermarket.

Howat outlined Litens ‘ strategy for integrating Dolz into its aftermarket portfolio, following its acquisition of the European water pump manufacturer about three years ago. Building on the approach used to establish the Litens brand in North America, the company is taking a phased approach to introducing Dolz to the market and building brand awareness. Howat, who oversees the company’s North American sales and marketing operations, said the strategy includes a marketing campaign launched this year, with plans to formally introduce the Dolz brand at AAPEX.

Litens’ ability to translate OE engineering expertise into aftermarket innovation begins with its extensive OE product knowledge and data, Howat explained. This expertise also enables the company to identify opportunities to improve upon existing OE designs.

As an example, Howat highlighted Litens’ newly patented Easy Button Latch technology, which simplifies tensioner installation by incorporating the locking mechanism directly into the component. The innovation eliminates installation challenges associated with conventional locking pins. It demonstrates how Litens leverages its engineering capabilities to develop aftermarket solutions that deliver practical benefits to technicians.

GM recalls 3.4 million pickups and SUVs over brake pump

On Sep. 6, General Motors notified dealers they will need to resolve an issue with a vacuum brake assist pump that makes it more difficult to engage the braking system and increases the risk for a crash. GM identified six models potentially afflicted with the defect between 2014 and 2018, totaling 3,456,111 vehicles in all. This includes two pickups—the Chevrolet Silverado (2014-2018) and GMC Sierra—and four SUVs, including the Cadillac Escalade (2015-2017), Chevrolet Suburban, Chevrolet Tahoe and GMC Yukon.

GM told CNN that the problem has resulted in 113 accidents  and 13 non-fatal injuries.

The problem appears to stem from excessive debris and sludge build-up on the vacuum pump filter screen as the engine oil lubricates it. This leads to a drop in vacuum and may necessitate more pressure applied to the brake pedal, create a “hard brake pedal,” and increase the time it takes to stop. Trucks and SUVs overdue for an oil change may be at a higher risk. Recalibrating the electronic brake control module to recognize lack of vacuum assist and activate hydraulic assist resolves the issue, GM says.

On the safety recall report, it’s noted that: “At all times, the brakes remain functional and exceed the requirements of S7.11 of Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) No. 135, ‘Light Vehicle Brake Systems.’”

The NHTSA opened the investigation last November and the Office of Defects Investigation received 111 hard brake reports from the various affected trucks and SUVs. Nine of the vehicles were involved in low-speed collisions, where it looks like the issue is more prevalent. The ABS system supplies supplemental hydraulic brake assist if vacuum drops, though at a lower level under low speeds.

GM is responsible for notifying owners, but you can also visit https://www.nhtsa.gov/recalls and enter your VIN to see if your vehicle needs to be brought in and repaired. The NHTSA Safety Issue ID is 19V645000. The dealership will reprogram Electronic Brake Control Module to fix the problem.

John Hitch is the editor-in-chief of Fleet Maintenance , providing maintenance management and technicians with the the latest information on the tools and strategies to keep their fleets' commercial vehicles moving. He is based out of Cleveland, Ohio, and was previously senior editor for FleetOwner. He previously wrote about manufacturing and advanced technology for IndustryWeek and New Equipment Digest.

Bosch Ventures invests in Asylon to Advance Autonomous Physical Operations

Accelerating expansion of autonomous robotic systems to strengthen the security and resilience of critical infrastructure

Physical AI advances security and inspection operations

Existing Bosch-Asylon technology collaboration combines alarm systems with autonomous robotics

Dr. Ingo Ramesohl, Co-Managing Director of Bosch Ventures: “By combining autonomous aerial and ground systems with intelligent software, Asylon is bringing robotics into demanding real-world environments.”

Christoph.Ferle@de.bosch.com

Boston & Norristown – Bosch Ventures, the corporate venture capital arm of the Bosch Group, and Asylon, a leader in autonomous physical operations, today announced an investment in Asylon to accelerate the development and deployment of autonomous, AI-enabled robotic systems for security, inspection, and other mission-critical physical operations.

Strengthening the resilience of critical infrastructure

Critical infrastructure operators face growing demands to monitor and secure complex physical assets around the clock. Asylon’s autonomous aerial and ground systems can continuously patrol sites, investigate security alerts, and provide real-time intelligence – helping operators detect potential threats earlier, respond faster, and reduce the need to send personnel into potentially hazardous situations.

The investment builds on an existing technology relationship between Asylon, Bosch and the Boston ecosystem. Currently, Asylon's DroneIQ platform integrates with alarm systems used within Bosch Building Technologies security solutions, enabling security events to initiate autonomous robotic response and investigation using Asylon's Guardian for aerial systems and Asylon’s DroneDog solution for ground robots. DroneDog is built on Boston Dynamics’ Spot robotic platform, combining advanced ground robotics with Asylon’s software and autonomous security capabilities.

Expanding Physical AI into real world operations

The integration connects existing security infrastructure with mobile autonomous systems capable of collecting real-time intelligence and extending the reach of human security teams.

“Asylon demonstrates the potential of Physical AI to make critical operations safer and more efficient. By combining autonomous aerial and ground systems with intelligent software, the team is bringing robotics into demanding real-world environments,” said Dr. Ingo Ramesohl, Co-Managing Director of Bosch Ventures.

The investment comes as Asylon expands its technology beyond automated security into a broader range of autonomous physical operations. The same combination of aerial and ground robotics, AI-enabled software and remote operational support can be applied to inspection and monitoring workflows across sectors including manufacturing, logistics, energy, data centers, defense-related aerospace. These applications can help organizations automate repetitive physical tasks, improve consistency and documentation, and increase operational efficiency.

"Bosch has been an invaluable technology partner for years, connecting traditional alarm infrastructure with autonomous robotic response," said Damon Henry, Founder and CEO of Asylon. "This investment deepens that relationship, providing technological and strategic value that will accelerate our path to scaling our solution to improve operations and reduce costs for customers around the world. They’re an ideal partner to deepen trust and boost operations for some of the most demanding companies in the world.”

TMD Friction adds brake reline program, new friction material

NASHVILLE, TN. TMD Friction made two announcements this week at the Technology and Maintenance Council’s annual meeting here, adding a new brake reline program and a new air disc brake friction material.

The first is a new engineering program designed to assist fleets in reducing brake reline costs. The Textar Fleet Assistance customer support program aims to reduce fleet maintenance costs by “pushing” brake relines out of the vehicle’s lifecycle.

According to TMD, the program includes direct communication to TMD engineers to help fleet maintenance managers analyze their brake lifecycles and costs, select the appropriate friction for each application and answer other brake questions.  Free, custom made lining wear gauges for both drum and disc brakes for any fleet are included using Textar products.

“Brake relines are one of the highest maintenance costs a fleet experiences and there is limited technical guidance out there to assist a fleet in making the optimal lining selection,” said Tom Green, managing director. “The Textar Fleet Assistance program has been developed to help fleets determine the different duty cycles within their fleet and select the appropriate grade of friction to minimize the maintenance expenses over the life of their vehicles.”

The program starts when the fleet manager fills out an information sheet that breaks down the fleet’s vehicle population into smaller “mini-fleets” that might have different brake lifecycles. Examples of mini-fleets could be tractors versus trailers, or long haul sleeper tractors versus short haul day cabs, or flatbed trailers versus van trailers.

TMD engineers will use the information to calculate if life improvement from Textar linings would push relines out of the lifecycles of each mini-fleet and how many total relines would be saved.  These calculations are based on extensive wear testing of aftermarket linings on specialized TMD laboratory dynamometers.

TMD also introduced a new air disc brake friction material at the show.

The Textar 3080 is engineered for applications where high torque levels are required to meet the FMVSS121 stopping distance regulations.

In dynamometer wear tests, two air disc friction materials with different effective coefficients of friction were tested by TMD. Results showed that with a higher effective coefficient of friction (0.38) the pad wears anywhere from 40% to 80% more than the lower friction pad (0.28).

The Textar T3080 air disc brake pad is the first of a new generation of low copper friction materials from TMD that are compliant to the upcoming 2014 and 2021 Environmental Regulations in the states of Washington and California, the company said.

According to Mobility Global ’s latest forecast, U.S. light-vehicle sales are expected to reach 16.1 million units in 2026 and 16.4 million by the end of the decade, remaining below the roughly 17 million annual sales levels that defined the market before the pandemic. Analysts speaking at a Mobility Global media briefing said affordability remains the single biggest challenge facing consumers, contributing to a fundamentally different market environment.

- Arnott Adds 10 Suspension Products for October

- Federated Auto Parts Announces Leadership Changes

- Auto Care Association Expands Demand Index

The discussion came at a pivotal moment for the industry. Automakers are navigating geopolitical instability, economic uncertainty, and shifting trade policies, even as consumers wrestle with the persistent problem of what they can afford.

Affordability Pressures Curb Recovery to Pre-Pandemic Volumes

The U.S. automotive market has remained depressed since the pandemic, with some of that due to supply chain shortages. But right now, the main reason Mobility Global doesn’t see the market returning to those previous levels and remaining below its potential is the affordability issue.

“We don’t see the U.S. returning to pre-pandemic levels of volumes,” said Peter Nagle, associate director for Americas demand forecasting. “Obviously, there is something constraining the market from those 17-million-unit thresholds that we routinely hit back in, say, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019.”

Policy Shifts Reshape Product Plans and Powertrain Mix

A myriad of factors have reshaped the automotive landscape in recent years. The past year has brought some significant changes to the U.S. regulatory and incentive framework — and in the compressed span of automotive timeframes. As emissions and fuel economy rules loosened, automakers rewrote product plans almost overnight.

“The resulting wave of battery-electric vehicle (BEV) cancellations may leave some suppliers wary of chasing future BEV programs,” said Eric Anderson, associate director for light vehicle powertrain forecasting. Even so, Mobility Global expects BEV assembly in North America to once again surpass 1 million units in 2027, according to its latest forecast.

The internal combustion engine vehicles and hybrids, however, the analysts said, are expected to remain central to the market as consumers continue to weigh cost, convenience and lifestyle in choosing their next car. Mobility Global forecasts North American assembly of full hybrid electric vehicles (FHEVs) to surpass 3 million units in 2027 — a 25% annual increase — with nearly a third of all North American light-vehicle assembly expected to be FHEV by 2030.

Regionalization Accelerates as China Shapes Global Strategies

The briefing also turned to China’s growing influence on the global automotive landscape. Analysts explored how conditions in China’s domestic market could shape automaker strategies worldwide. They pointed to a broader industry move toward regionalization and de-globalization.

“The auto industry is moving toward three major regional islands,” said Joe Langley, director of research and analysis. “North America, Europe and Asia, and automakers will increasingly have to build where they sell and design for the regions they serve. The difficult part is doing that while costs continue to rise.”

And there is no longer one global recipe for success, Langley added.

Jake Brake turns 60, but conceived 90 years ago

The Jacobs compression release engine brake, or "Jake brake," is now in its 60th year of service, with more than 9 million of the systems manufactured by 2019. The   compression release brake   system, which turns the engine into an air compressor, has helped countless truckers slow down their truck by shifting stopping energy from the brakes and converting it into hot air released through the exhaust.

This has spared wear and tear on brakes the world over, extending their service life. More importantly, by reducing the friction on brakes during long downhill stretches, the Jake brake keeps them from failing when the trucker needs them most.

And it all started when the founding father of U.S. diesel engines nearly lost his life due to failing brakes and an inopportune train schedule.

Ninety years ago, Clessie Cummins, founder and namesake of the engine manufacturer, Cummins Inc. , along with two compatriots, hopped in a diesel truck specially outfitted with bunks, storage and stove for an incredulous journey across America to test the endurance of diesel trucks. That 3,214-mile trip from New York to California trailblazed the way for every long-hauler who followed, all for the fuel cost of $11.22, or $194.15 in today’s dollars. But it almost cost Cummins his life.

Dashing down the Cajon Pass on the old Route 66 in California, which has an apex of 3,777 ft. above sea level, Cummins saw a train roaring across the road below. As legend goes, he barely missed T-boning the caboose as the truck crossed the tracks. In the decades that followed, Cummins kept that near-miss — and how to avoid another — close to his heart.

“In the ’50s, when he finally retired from Cummins, he spent some time working on that and trying to figure out how to turn the engine into some sort of compressive brake,” explained Steve Ernest, vice president, Engineering and Business Development for Jacobs Vehicle Systems , the company that formed in 1961 to commercialize the braking innovation.

“As you’re going down along a hill, you get some push back from the engine on the truck. That way the foundation brakes are nice and cool and ready to go in the event you do have to do an emergency stop or really slow down very quickly,” Ernest explained.

This additional retardation helps slow the vehicle, reducing the friction on the foundation brakes. Ernest said the Jake Brake extends brake life by two to three times.

While Volvo uses its own compression brake, Jacobs has 100% penetration on Detroit Diesel and Cummins X15 engines and 92% on Navistar’s A26 engine. A study of International trucks found the $2,500 cost of the system is recouped upon resale.

Owner-operator Grant E. Sheldon found the Jake Brake saves him $1,000 per year in brake maintenance costs.

“I use the Jake Brake like crazy and because of that, I easily double the life of my foundation brakes,” said the Kentucky-based driver with 50 years of trucking experience.

Jacobs has continued to innovate with such solutions as Cylinder Deactivation Technology (CDA) , which can cut fuel consumption by 5% while reducing NOx emissions as well.

John Hitch is the editor-in-chief of Fleet Maintenance , providing maintenance management and technicians with the the latest information on the tools and strategies to keep their fleets' commercial vehicles moving. He is based out of Cleveland, Ohio, and was previously senior editor for FleetOwner. He previously wrote about manufacturing and advanced technology for IndustryWeek and New Equipment Digest.

A Detroit Free Press article explores how tailoring vehicle sensors to individual body types could one day aid in crash safety for those involved in collisions.

The article centers on the belief of vehicle safety researchers and engineers that “the next frontier of safety focuses on catering the front seat safety system to the human behind the wheel.”

“At the urging of regulators in Europe and North America, automakers and their supplier partners plan to move into occupant classification ― using vehicle sensors to identify the approximate height and weight of drivers so the safety systems protect them more effectively,” the article states.

Erin Keating, Cox Automotive executive analyst, notes that a 5-star safety rating in the U.S. is the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s standardized measure to inform consumers how a vehicle performs in a defined crash safety test; however, it doesn’t show how the vehicles perform for every individual.

“The auto industry is starting to move beyond those constraints, Keating said,” according to the article. “Instead of trying to build a perfect set of dummies for every scenario, the plan is adaptive safety, where vehicle systems ‘sense’ who is driving [and] adjust protection accordingly. That’s how you start to close the gap, she said, between a standardized rating and a more individualized outcome.”

Lisa Furton, a vehicle performance owner for occupant protection at General Motors, adds that “collecting accurate passenger data and adjusting vehicle protective systems accordingly is safety’s next frontier,” according to the article.

Dr. Steward Wang, professor emeritus of surgery at the Trauma Burn Center at the University of Michigan, notes in the article that personalized protection systems in vehicles are still years, if not decades, away. The Free Press reports that Wang spent 14 years as a principal investigator for the multidisciplinary Crash Injury Research Engineering Network (CIREN), a government-industry-academiaresearch consortium.

“We’re still a number of decades away from getting a good human body model that can be predictive of all injuries. It’s pretty good now, but they don’t get everybody in the population,” Wang said, according to the article. “You need more detailed information about what the end results are, the specific injuries that occur. The cars need to make it out there into the real world, and unfortunately live people are the real crash dummies.”

The article adds that, “despite technological innovations and advancements in data collection of crashes,” differences in injury patterns and severity between men and women of different sizes, even in the same crash conditions, mean there’s “‘no clear solution’ to protect everyone equally.”

However, “Wang agrees that getting more body types involved in the crash test scenarios that automakers have to pass could improve safety,” the article states. “If the driver isn’t secure because their body type does not allow them to sit behind the wheel the same way a dummy does, the vehicle ‘doesn’t know,’ Wang said. And without advanced sensor technology and some degree of artificial intelligence, a vehicle ‘can’t know.'”

Wang added, according to the article: “The thought is, if it is safer for some, it should be safer for most.”

Jason Hallman, senior manager of Toyota’s Collaborate Safety Research Center, told the Free Press that today’s vehicles “rely on a robust system that covers a broad spectrum of the population generally,” and “more data needs to be collected, analyzed, and verified before making adjustments to the vehicles themselves.”

Jessica Jermakian, senior vice president for vehicle research at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS), adds: “What we’re ultimately looking for is not an individual restraint system tailored to each individual person — though the Holy Grail would be one that is somewhat adaptable — but one that is generally robust, that even when it doesn’t perform perfectly like the crash test, it’s still doing a good job.”

EPA copper-free brake initiative moves to next phase

With the first phase of the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Copper-Free Brake Initiative coming to a close at the end of the year, Bendix Commercial Vehicle Systems reminds fleets and owner-operators to make sure they’re keeping up with the necessary changes in aftermarket air disc brake (ADB) friction formulation.

“It’s important that fleets, distributors, and everyone who does brake pad changes is aware of what’s going on with various Bendix replacement pads and labeling,” said Keith McComsey, Bendix director of Air Disc Brake and Systems. “And with the significant increase in ADB adoption over the past decade, there’s a particular interest in ADB pad changes.”

In January 2015, organizations within the automotive and commercial vehicle industries – including trucking – signed onto the Copper-Free Brake Initiative, along with the EPA and the Environmental Council of the States. This action was taken because copper from stormwater runoff can be harmful to the environment, affecting plants and animals – and when used in brake pads, it makes its way into the air and water through the fine dust released from friction during braking.

In 2010, according to EPA estimates, vehicular braking in California alone released 1.3 million pounds of copper into the environment. That year, both California and Washington passed laws reducing the amount of copper permitted in brake pads.

B-Level compliance, or phase 2, of the initiative takes effect on Jan. 1, 2021, and limits the amount of copper to no more than 5% by weight. Other material limits remain unchanged. In January 2025, copper’s limit will drop to 0.5% – one-half of 1% – by weight for N-Level compliance. The agreement also commits participants to take steps to educate the automotive and trucking industries on the changes and provides guidelines for marking and labeling friction material packaging and products.

“Even though many Bendix friction materials have been compliant with the 2021 standards for a long time, some older aftermarket ADB pads will be phasing out of compliance at the end of the year,” McComsey said. “For customers currently using these, we’ve been including postcards with the replacement kits letting them know about the change and pointing them to the compliant friction.”

The A-Level-compliant frictions, which include both the Bendix BX275 OE-level friction and the aftermarket BA235, will become obsolete. The suitable B-Level copper-compliant replacements are the Bendix BX276 and BX283 pads, which are OE-level pads already available in the North American market. Both will remain compliant through 2024, while providing longer friction life and meeting FMVSS-121 stopping distance and park hold requirements. Bendix will also launch the BA236 pad in 2021, an aftermarket friction that will be B-Level copper-compliant through 2024.

Bendix parts and replacement kit numbers involved are:

BX275 – obsolete Dec. 31, 2020

BA235 – obsolete Dec. 31, 2020

BX276 – available; compliant through 2024

BX283 – available; compliant through 2024

BA236 – coming in 2021; compliant through 2024

Bendix wheel-end solutions include air disc and drum brake systems, automatic slack adjusters, spring brakes, friction, and remanufactured brake shoes that provide lower total cost of ownership while delivering on safety, stopping power, and reliability. Bendix helps fleets and drivers in the areas most critical to their success by improving vehicle performance and efficiency, and by backing its products with unparalleled post-sales support. By strengthening return on investment in the technologies that improve vehicle and driver safety, Bendix supports safer North American roads for all who share them.

“When Phase 3 of the initiative rolls around on Jan. 1, 2025, Bendix will be ready for that too,” McComsey said. “We’re already engineering copper-compliant ADB friction for the most stringent level, with plans for production to begin well in advance of the deadline.”

The Mevotech team looked at the complete brake job, and the time technicians spend completing it. When bay time is valuable, engineering a product with the repair process in mind can help reduce unnecessary steps and support a more efficient installation.

“Stopping performance, durability, elimination of rust build-up, fade resistance, noise control and braking characteristics remain essential. Those are non-negotiable,” Stothers said. “But we believe product performance should be evaluated from the moment the technician opens the box, not simply from the moment the vehicle leaves the bay.”

“TTX Brake Service Kits are one result of that thinking. Depending on the application, a kit can contain up to 40 premium components, providing technicians with hardware and service items that might otherwise have to be sourced separately or reused. Every part of the abutment clips for example is stainless steel and rubber coated,” added Baldev Hayer, director of brakes.

The contents vary by application and can include abutment clips, slide pins, boots and bracket bolts, along with items such as wear sensors and lubricants. Some kits also provide tools or service items such as a wire brush and caliper hangers.

The number of pieces in the kit is less important than the thinking behind them. The goal is to give technicians more of what they may need when the repair begins, helping reduce time spent sourcing additional hardware and allowing them to focus on completing the job.

That thinking is not limited to brakes. Across its portfolio, Mevotech continues to look for opportunities to make installation more efficient and help address challenges technicians encounter in the bay. Labor Saver designs can include application-specific fasteners, installation tools and hardware, while complete control arm assemblies can help reduce the number of separate steps involved in a repair. Features such as greaseable self-lubricating powder metal bearings are another example of engineering being applied with durability and service life in mind.

For Mevotech , these efforts start with understanding the repair and the challenges technician’s encounter. Technician feedback, field experience and the knowledge of teams across the company help identify opportunities where a product or the installation experience may be improved. Innovation helps fuel that engineering process, but being different for the sake of being different is never the objective. The focus is on creating meaningful value, whether that means addressing a failure point, improving durability or performance, simplifying installation or helping a technician save time in the bay.

Supporting the technician also extends beyond the physical product. Technical documentation, training and installation content are an important part of helping technicians understand the product and complete the repair with confidence. As vehicles and repairs become increasingly complex, providing useful and accessible technical resources has become another important part of supporting the people working on those vehicles every day.

That support is also a team effort. Bringing a product to market requires engineering, product, technical services, manufacturing, supply chain, sales and other teams across Mevotech to work together. Each brings a different perspective, but the objective remains consistent: develop products and provide resources that can help technicians do their jobs effectively.

TTX Brakes brought many of those capabilities together by applying decades of engineering experience to a new category. The result is a brake program built around purpose-designed friction solutions for different applications and duty cycles, while also accounting for the complete brake job, from installation hardware and technical support to manufacturing and distribution.

Looking Beyond the Next Category

That question is: Where does Mevotech go next? Each expansion adds another layer of experience to the development platform behind the products. As Mevotech approaches its 45th anniversary, the company sees an opportunity to build carefully on what its teams have learned, while continuing to listen to technicians, customers and distribution partners.

While TTX Brakes is the latest example of that process, where Mevotech applies it next will help shape the next stage of the company’s growth.

The essential economy is not a category on a spreadsheet, Ford CEO Jim Farley said during the “ACCELERATE the Essential Economy” event Wednesday.

“It might be a grandfather, an aunt, or even a kid,” Farley said.

The essential economy is made up of industries that are comprised of skilled workers , such as, construciton, manufacturing, energy, public services, transportation and logistics.

Farley added that the nation has looked past skilled jobs for decades and the economy is at risk because of this.

“It is not going to be solved overnight, but we are going to get a lot more done if we do it together,” Farley said.

The first ACCELERATE event was held last year. Farley said the event set three priorities: gather facts, train more people, and break stereotypes.

The Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades, formed following last year’s ACCELERATE event, released “ The State of America’s Skilled Trades: A National Report ” Wednesday. It found that training programs are producing 55 workers for every 100 needed in the skilled trades.

Ford, BlackRock, Google, and Carhartt founded the Alliance for America’s Skilled Trades earlier this year. Fourteen new corporations were announced as joining Wednesday.

Farley says that more than $1 billion has been invested in training for skilled jobs by those who attended Wednesday’s event.

This includes a $5 million investment by Ford and Bloomberg Philanthropies to modernize auto technician programs at two schools within Detroit, with plans to expand the program nationally.

The Ad Council is also working on a national social impact program to change the perception of skilled jobs, Farley said.

“My grandfather was an hourly worker for Ford and his skilled trade job at Ford put my mom through college,” Farley said. “These jobs are good jobs; they changed America, and they can change America again.”

Ruth Porat, Alphabet and Google CEO, said that after touring skilled worker training facilities across the nation, she’s learned how important the jobs are to communities.

Workers in facilities often told her it was not a job, but a career.

“I was in the middle of the country, and somebody said to me that, ‘Our greatest export has been our children because they don’t see hope in my town. They don’t see a career for themselves in my town, and now they do,’” Porat said.

Larry Fink, CEO of BlackRock, said that as the largest investor of retirement savings, his job is to focus on the long term.

“I have never been more optimistic about the United States in my entire career,” Fink said.

He said that rebuilding the essential economy is a “huge investment opportunity to rebuild America.”

“These men and women can have a career in a trade where they can have a middle-class job and throughout their career they will be able to save enough for their retirement,” Fink said.

Hopefully, the workers will reinvest back into America, he added.

Linda Hubbard, Carhartt CEO and president, said her company has celebrated and valued the skilled trades since its start.

“We’ve been waiting for decades for everybody to get on board,” Hubbard said.

She added that it felt like skilled trade workers were invisible.

“If youngsters see themselves in these roles, in these very cool jobs that are building, growing, making, fixing America and the world, if they see themselves in it, their families will encourage them to explore it more,” Hubbard said.

Farley said it is important that the nation starts investing in these jobs because it will mean longer wait times and higher costs for essential needs, such as vehicle repair.

“It is a solvable thing,” Farley said.

During the event, Farley directed the audience to data in the new report, saying high-quality apprenticeships that included apprentice support were more likely to lead more workers into the essential economy. He added that additional support could be health care or transportation.

The report found traditional training methods had only about a 50% completion rate. It also found that high-quality apprenticeship programs have a completion rate of more than 90%.

Farley said finishing a program can be difficult if you aren’t getting paid and you have a family at home that needs health care and food.

“We need the social programs to help and support, and we need the programs to be accredited and we employers to be connected to these apprenticeships so that the people have a job,” Farley said.

Featured image: Ford CEO Jim Farley speaking during the 2026 ACCELERATE the Essential Economy event on Sept. 30./Courtesy of Ford.

Long before streaming platforms, smartphones, and social media, audiences watched movies without a single spoken word. Silent films relied entirely on visuals to tell the story, and people followed along just fine. Visuals carried the message then, and they still do today.

In today’s automotive aftermarket, images remain one of the most important ways products are communicated. Whether customers are browsing an ecommerce site, searching a distributor catalog, or comparing products online, visuals often influence purchasing decisions before a single line of product data is read.

As digital commerce continues to grow, managing visual content has become just as important as creating it.

Managing More Content Than Ever

Manufacturers today manage far more than product images. They are responsible for videos, installation guides, lifestyle photography, logos, technical documents, 360 degree imagery, marketing materials, and more.

As product portfolios expand and content is needed across marketplaces, ecommerce platforms, and distribution partners, keeping those assets organized and accessible is becoming more difficult.

The challenge is no longer creating content. It’s managing it.

Companies are asking questions such as:

• Which image is the most current version?

• Has the latest logo been distributed everywhere?

• Are product photos consistent across partner websites?

• Who has access to the right files?

• How do we get the right assets to customers and partners without creating more work?

Without a clear process, teams can spend more time looking for assets than actually using them.

Keeping Content Consistent

One of the biggest challenges is maintaining consistency across channels.

An updated image may be available internally while an older version continues to appear on websites, distributor portals, catalogs, and marketing materials. The result can be inconsistent branding, outdated information, and confusion throughout the supply chain.

This is one reason companies are turning to centralized digital asset management systems that provide a single source of truth and make it easier to keep content current across multiple channels.

Digital Asset Management Solutions such as TecAlliance Pixey are helping companies address this challenge by giving them greater control over digital assets while reducing some of the manual work involved in keeping content current across teams and trading partners.

A single product image may need to be published in multiple sizes, formats, and resolutions depending on where it is being used.

Historically, teams have managed these variations manually, creating duplicate files and increasing the risk of errors. Today, systems can automatically generate different versions from a single master file, including resizing, format conversion, border application, and optimization.

Instead of maintaining dozens of versions of the same asset, teams can manage one source file and let the system handle many of the variations required for different channels.

As asset libraries grow, finding the right content becomes a challenge of its own.

Companies are relying more heavily on metadata to organize assets using product attributes, brands, vehicle applications, campaigns, and other business specific information. A well-structured metadata strategy can turn a digital asset library from simple storage into a searchable business resource.

For the aftermarket, where product relationships and application data can be complex, being able to find the right content is becoming just as important as storing it.

Managing and storing content is only part of the challenge. Manufacturers and suppliers also need to deliver that content to distributors, retailers, marketplaces, sales teams, marketers, and other partners, often in different formats and through different methods.

Digital asset management is therefore moving beyond storage and organization to include how content is shared and distributed throughout the supply chain.

Organizations using platforms such as Pixey can more effectively manage, distribute, and deliver the right content to the right people across the supply chain.

Visual content has always influenced how people understand products and make decisions. What’s changing is the scale and complexity of managing that content.

Across the aftermarket, companies are dealing with more products, more channels, more partners, and more digital content than ever before. Keeping assets synchronized, creating the right versions, making content easy to find, and getting it where it needs to go are becoming important parts of managing product information.

Ultimately, effective digital asset management is about making it easier to find the right content, keep it current, and get it where it needs to go, so businesses can spend less time managing content and more time using it.

2024 Brake Safety Week: What fleets and drivers should know

Another year, another chance for the trucking industry to focus on brake safety. Let’s go over what fleets and drivers need to know for this year’s Brake Safety Week.

What is Brake Safety Week?

According to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance , Brake Safety Week is a commercial motor vehicle and driver inspection and regulatory compliance enforcement initiative, a brake-safety awareness and outreach opportunity, and a brake-related inspection and violation data collection project. Each year, this event is hosted by CVSA.

This means that inspections will be conducted throughout Brake Safety Week with particular focus on brake performance. Vehicles can be taken out of service if brake violations are discovered.

When is Brake Safety Week?

Brake Safety Week this year will be August 25-31. According to past CVSA records, Brake Safety Week typically occurs at the end of August.

Unlike Brake Safety Day , another CVSA event—the date of which goes unannounced until after the event has occurred—fleets have time and the knowledge needed to prepare for Brake Safety Week.

How should fleets prepare for Brake Safety Week?

The emphasis of Brake Safety Week this year will be on the condition of brake linings and pads. Inspectors will be looking for excessive wear in the brake linings and pads, particularly cracks, according to Jim Ward, senior safety manager at Transervice Logistics .

Ward said that one red flag that drivers may not think twice about but inspectors will is rubbing air lines.

“Those [rubbing air lines] get written up a lot,” Ward said. “If you have two brake lines—which some of them are rubber, others are like a poly material—what happens is those two hoses have a lot of pressure going through them, and they're sitting right next to each other. So over time, with the vibration of the truck, they tend to rub against each other, and they can start leaving little marks on each other. Sometimes they'll wear down far enough to actually put a big chafe into the hose. To me, that's something that's overlooked. It may look fine, but if those two hoses are touching, you're going to get written up for it because you should make sure that they’re kept separated.”

See also: CVSA releases results of 2024 Brake Safety Day

To prepare for Brake Safety Week, Ward suggests focusing on pre- and post-trip inspections as well as preventive maintenance .

“The most important thing is PM and pre-trip inspections,” Ward said. “Make sure that the trucks are PM’d on a regular basis … When you're a driver, the most important thing for you to continue to do is pre-trip. Pre-trip inspect your vehicle because it saves your life and the people in front of you or people around you.”

What will the results of Brake Safety Week be?

According to CVSA, Brake Safety Week in 2022 resulted in 13.3% out-of-service violations. This decreased to 12.6% in 2023. This trend may continue in 2024, however, it’s also possible that safety technology will result in more accurate brake performance inspections.

This year, CVSA announced that performance-based brake testers (PBBTs) will be used in some jurisdictions during Brake Safety Week. PBBTs are machines that test brake performance. They measure the slow-speed brake force and weight at each wheel of a vehicle, add up the total vehicle brake force, and divide it by the total vehicle weight to determine overall vehicle braking efficiency.

It’s difficult to speculate, but the use of this technology could affect the percentage of out-of-service violations with more accurate measurements of brake performance.

Why is Brake Safety Week important?

According to CVSA, brake violations comprise the largest percentage of out-of-service violations cited during roadside inspections. CVSA cites that in last year’s International Roadcheck , brake violations were the top vehicle violation, comprising 25.2% of all vehicle out-of-service violations during those three days.

Brake Safety Week serves as a reminder to drivers and fleet managers of the importance of vehicle maintenance and provides an opportunity for law enforcement to highlight the importance of brake safety for all.

Bosch Korea confirmed as Exclusive Global Mobility Insights Partner for FISITA World Mobility Summit 2026

Partnership brings Bosch’s technology leadership to the Summit’s dedicated Global Mobility Insights Session, as senior mobility leaders gather in Korea to explore the complexities of mobility

LONDON, UK / SEOUL, REPUBLIC OF KOREA, FISITA, the global alliance advancing the technology of mobility, today announced that Bosch Korea has signed on as the exclusive Global Mobility Insights Partner for the FISITA World Mobility Summit 2026. The Summit takes place 4–5 November 2026 at the Rolling Hills Hotel in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi, Republic of Korea, hosted by FISITA in partnership with the Korean Society of Automotive Engineers (KSAE).

As Global Mobility Insights Partner, Bosch Korea will sponsor the Summit’s dedicated Global Mobility Insights Session, contributing to one of the event’s most important dialogues on the future direction of mobility technology and engineering. The partnership reflects Bosch’s long-standing commitment to innovation, collaboration and thought leadership across the global mobility ecosystem.

Hosted by FISITA President ChangHwan Kim, Executive Vice President of Hyundai Motor Company and held under the theme “Embracing the Complexities of Mobility,” the 2026 Summit is FISITA’s annual leadership forum, bringing together senior executives, CTOs and R&D leaders from the world’s most significant automotive and mobility organisations, including Hyundai Motor Group, Toyota, Xiaomi Auto and Bosch, alongside the presidents of FISITA’s member engineering societies.

Over two days of strategic discussion, thought leadership and high-level networking, delegates will examine the strategic forces shaping mobility’s future, including software-defined vehicles and AI, battery technology and electrification, energy infrastructure, autonomous driving and regulation and regional perspectives from Asia, Europe and North America.

Recognised as one of the most exclusive gatherings in the international mobility leadership calendar, the FISITA World Mobility Summit provides a unique environment for senior executives, engineers, researchers and industry decision-makers to exchange ideas, challenge assumptions and explore practical pathways towards a safe, sustainable and affordable mobility future.

“We are delighted to welcome Bosch Korea as our Global Mobility Insights Partner for the FISITA World Mobility Summit 2026. Bosch is recognised worldwide for its engineering excellence, technology leadership and commitment to advancing mobility innovation and having them join us is a real vote of confidence in what this Summit is built to do, bring the industry’s most significant decision-makers into one room, in Korea, to work through the questions that matter most”

– Chris Mason, Chief Executive Officer, FISITA.

“The Summit is intentionally designed to bring together the people responsible for making some of the most important decisions in global mobility and partnerships like this are exactly what allow us to keep raising the bar for what it delivers, for our members and for the wider industry.”

“The future of mobility will not be defined by a single technology, a single company or a single market, success will depend on our ability to embrace complexity and bring together expertise from across the entire mobility ecosystem. That belief sits at the heart of the FISITA World Mobility Summit 2026 and it is exactly why I am so pleased to welcome Bosch Korea as our Global Mobility Insights Partner”

– ChangHwan Kim, President, FISITA and Executive Vice President, Hyundai Motor Company

“Bosch’s presence in this session reflects the kind of cross-industry collaboration our sector needs. As we explore topics ranging from software-defined vehicles and AI to battery technologies, automated driving and energy infrastructure, the complexity we face is not a problem to be eliminated, it is a reality to be embraced together and that is what we will do in Korea this November.”

“Bosch is proud to support the FISITA World Mobility Summit 2026 as Global Mobility Insights Partner. The Summit has established itself as one of the most respected forums for senior technology leaders across the global mobility community, exactly the audience we want to be in dialogue with as the industry sets the direction for the next generation of mobility,”

“The theme ‘Embracing the Complexities of Mobility’ strongly reflects the realities facing our industry today. Delivering sustainable, safe and intelligent mobility requires collaboration across technologies, industries and regions and we look forward to contributing our insights and engaging with industry peers in Korea this November.”

– Marcello Lusuardi, President of Robert Bosch Korea.

Other organisations attending the FISITA World Mobility Summit include: BYD, Changan, Denso, JATCO, Maersk, Mann+Hummel, NIO, Toyota Motor Corporation, Xiaomi and Geely.

Further details on the FISITA World Mobility Summit 2026, including registration and the full programme, are available at www.fisita.com/summit

At one time, brake pad wear sensors were a pretty simple matter: the sensor was just a spring steel tab that was mounted on the backing plate and bent at a right angle. The tab was as long as the minimum depth for the pad’s friction material, so when the pad wore down to that minimum depth the tab would drag on the brake rotor and cause an unmistakable metal-on-metal screech that would alert the driver that it was time for new brakes. Unfortunately, many drivers don’t even know what that screech means or may not notice it in a vehicle that’s got a lot of sound deadening, and by the time they bring their car into the shop the rotors are already chewed up (and the vehicle is very unsafe to drive).

- Toyota RAV4 2006-2013 Alignment

- ZF 6HP Valve Body Identification

- Do We Need New Rules for ADAS Repair?

While many brake pads, both OEM and aftermarket, still feature these simple wear indicators, newer systems are more sophisticated. That means giving a driver a heads-up long before the pads get down to minimum thickness and start damaging the rotors through metal-to-metal contact.

Brake Wear Sensor Designs

Older brake pad wear sensors consisted of a loop of wire embedded in the friction material at a certain depth, with a low amount of current running through it  and the sensor looped into the vehicle’s ABS circuit and processor. This sensor had a known resistance value; when resistance would be above 2000 ohms, a rectifier circuit would read that as an open circuit and would light up an indicator on the dash. These designs could be prone to corrosion or physical damage (sometimes just due to heat from the brakes), and it was always recommended that the sensor be replaced along with the pads when it was time for a brake job.

Newer sensor designs are capable of actually giving a driver an estimate of the number of miles that are left on the pads. The key difference is that they’re designed with two resistor circuits in parallel with each other. The first circuit is set at a higher position in the sensor, with the second in a lower position. When the first circuit is broken, the parallel design means that the resistance will increase. If the second wire is broken, the circuit is then read as open, triggering the warning light on the dash.

With these two-stage sensor systems, the first circuit usually won’t trigger a warning light. Instead, the system starts to calculate remaining pad life with information about wheel rotational speed, mileage, brake pressure, brake rotor and pad temperature and total brake operating time. Splicing wires together to bypass the sensor won’t work – the module confirms the sensor is working by  passing voltage through the circuit. Splicing wires together would mean the system would read it as an open circuit and would set the dash warning light.

Most vehicles will have one sensor for the front axle and one for the rear, although some might be equipped with a sensor for each wheel. Some systems are designed for two-stage warnings, sometimes with a yellow indicator light for the first stage and a red light for when brake pad replacement is imminent.

Considering that the wire loop is destroyed as part of normal wear, it’s necessary to replace the sensor when doing a brake job. Even if the customer gets the vehicle in early and the sensors haven’t been triggered, the old sensors will already be partially worn and could have damaged leads. Be sure you’re using the proper sensors for the vehicle’s year/make/model, as different sensors have different lead lengths, connector types and mounting designs.

For Mercedes-Benz, Audi, Volkswagen, Mini and BMW models, it’s necessary to perform a reset after replacing the pads and sensors.

While the process can vary from one year/make/model to another, a typical reset might involve these steps:

Turn on the ignition by pressing the start/stop button once or twice without your foot on the brake pedal (don’t start the engine).

Wait for all the dashboard lights and chimes to finish.

Find the BC button on the turn signal stalk to cycle through until it displays time and mileage/trip odometer.

Press and hold the odometer reset button until you see a service menu on the instrument cluster.

Use the stalk button to scroll through the options until you see the Brake Pad Service icon.

Press and hold the button again until “Reset?” appears.

Release the button quickly, then press and hold again until the reset occurs and the mileage counter is updated.

For BMW models, this may have to be done through the vehicle’s iDrive system.

Installing the Replacement Sensors

Installation is usually a pretty simple affair. Locate the wire that runs from the brake pad to the wheel well housing or junction box, and undo any fender liner clips or protective access doors. Unplug the sensor by pushing the plastic release tab on its connector. If there are any guide clips along the brake line, carefully unclip them. The sensor can then be pulled or pried from its slot on the interior brake pad. Installation is the reverse of removal, as you push the new sensor head firmly into the slot on the pad and route the wire along the exact same path as before. Be sure to reinstall any clips, rubber grommets or brackets.

Recall Roundup: Steering, brake, frame, and fire risks prompt truck recalls

NHTSA recalls affect commercial vehicles from Volvo Trucks, Paccar, Orange EV, and Shyft.

Fleets should inspect affected vehicles and complete recall repairs to reduce safety risks.

Steering, brake, frame, and electrical defects can increase crash or fire risks if left unaddressed.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently issued recall notices for commercial vehicles, including brands from Shyft Group, Volvo Trucks North America (VTNA), and more.

Owners of the affected vehicles should be contacted via U.S. mail over the next two months, but fleet and independent owners of these vehicles can contact the NHTSA Safety Hotline at 888-327-4236 or visit nhtsa.gov for more details. More information about each recall can be found below.

Orange EV models’ frame rails may crack

Orange EV is recalling certain 2023-2024 e-Triever, 2020-2023 T-Series Tandem Terminal Truck, and 2024-2026 Husk-e Tandem Terminal vehicles. Improper welding may cause frame rails to crack, leading to rail separation. A detached rail can cause a loss of control, increasing the risk of injury.

This recall potentially affects 24 vehicles. Dealers will inspect and repair or replace the frame rails as necessary. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed July 22. Owners may contact Orange EV customer service at 866-688-5223. Orange EV's number for this recall is 2026-SRC-02 .

Paccar models’ incorrectly installed quick-release valve

Paccar is recalling certain 2026-2027 Peterbilt 579 and 2027 Kenworth T680 tractors. The trailer air connection quick release valve in the air brake system may have been incorrectly installed, which can cause the trailer to become unstable after the driver applies the brakes. As such, these vehicles fail to comply with the requirements of Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard number 121, "Air Brake Systems." An incorrectly installed quick release valve that does not function properly can increase the risk of a crash.

This recall potentially affects eight vehicles. Paccar inspected and reinstalled the valves, as necessary. All affected tractors have been repaired; therefore, no owner notification letters are necessary. Owners may contact Peterbilt's customer service at 940-591-4220 and Kenworth's customer service at 425-828-5888. Paccar's number for this recall is 26PACC .

Clark: Strategies to combat diesel price volatility and protect fleet margins

From luxury to standard: How satellite radio grew into an essential driver retention amenity

Utilimaster models’ strobe light may circuit

Shyft Group is recalling certain 2016, 2019, and 2021 Utilimaster Velocity vehicles. Water may enter an improperly sealed strobe light and cause a short circuit. An electrical short increases the risk of a fire.

This recall potentially affects 563 vehicles. Owners are advised to remove the control module for the strobe light. The remedy is currently under development. Interim owner notification letters explaining the safety risk were expected to be mailed July 17. Another notice will be sent once the remedy becomes available. Owners may contact Shyft customer service at 800-237-7806. Shyft's number for this recall is 26-06 .

VTNA models’ loss of steering control from loose steering arm fasteners

Volvo Trucks North America (VTNA) is recalling certain 2026 Volvo VHD, VNL (4), VNR (4), VN, and VAH vehicles. The steering knuckles may have been manufactured with insufficiently tightened steering arms. A loose steering arm can result in a loss of vehicle steering control, increasing the risk of a crash.

This recall potentially affects 3,794 vehicles. Dealers will inspect and tighten the fasteners between the steering arm and steering knuckle, as necessary. Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed September 7. Owners may contact Volvo Trucks' customer service at 800-528-6586. Volvo Trucks' number for this recall is RVXX2607 .

She has a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree in creative writing from Truman State University and a master of Fine Arts degree in writing from Lindenwood University. She is currently based in Missouri.
